title: What We're Reading, Incorruptible by Eric Ries
author: Ashley Murphy
summary: Murphy reports three takeaways from a fireside chat with Eric Ries about his book Incorruptible, and the through line is that organizational decay is a leadership problem with a name people avoid using. Ries asks the group to think of a beloved brand that got bought, went public, or took the big check and then got worse, then argues that the polite labels we reach for, bureaucracy or mission drift, are euphemisms their grandparents would have skipped in favor of corruption. Naming it plainly, he holds, restores the urgency the situation deserves. The second takeaway addresses why stated values are met with skepticism, which Murphy reframes as experience rather than cynicism, since most employees have watched lobby wall values function as a smokescreen, with Enron's integrity signage as the standing example. The remedy is unglamorous proof through action, and the payoff is practical: leadership alignment, recruiting, and fundraising all get easier once trust is real. The third takeaway concerns ethical costs that resist measurement, prompted by a member question about building with AI, where Ries refuses both the reassurance that it is fine and the advice to opt out entirely. His answer is to move toward the more trustworthy option where one genuinely exists and to start measuring the cost that others call unmeasurable. Murphy closes by questioning the assumed split between the kind business decision and the smart one.
points: The central rhetorical move is lexical, replacing softened terms like mission drift with the older and blunter word corruption to restore urgency.
Employee skepticism about company values is reframed as earned experience rather than cynicism, since most people have seen posted values used as cover.
Ries's argument for integrity is partly instrumental, since a trustworthy brand eases leadership alignment, hiring, and fundraising.
On AI he refuses both escapes offered to operators, neither absolving the externalities nor recommending withdrawal from building.
His practical test for any cost called too hard to measure is to start measuring it, on the grounds that operators routinely measure hard things they have decided matter.
quotes: It's easy to take a pessimistic point of view on the nature of companies. We've all seen enough headlines, or witnessed enough bad behavior, to build an assumption that some level of corruption is inevitable.

Eric asked us all to think of a brand you loved that got bought, went public, or took the big check — and then got worse. How would we name the problem? Bureaucracy? Mission drift? In Eric’s opinion, our grandparents wouldn’t have struggled to name this issue. They would have simply called it corruption.
As a leader, when you tell your team about your company values, many people are skeptical. It’s not because they’re cynical; it’s because they’re experienced.
In order to overcome this, leaders have to do real, unglamorous work to prove through their actions that their values matter.
The externalities of AI building are real, and they aren’t small. By building, you’re implicated in them.

His actual answer was less comfortable and more doable: move your business to the more trustworthy option whenever you can genuinely find one, and when someone tells you a cost is “too hard to measure”… get to work measuring it.

In our personal lives, it's normal to feel drawn to the people and organizations that make kind choices. So why do we create a false dichotomy between the kind business decision and the smart one at work?
Maybe the kind choice and the smart one were never really separate — and building our organizations to be incorruptible is how we stop pretending they are.
